new_statements.quote: Stress still needs to be investigated in greater detail. However, some preliminary findings shall be outlined here. Stress is free in the sense that its position cannot be predicted for any word from general phonological rules. Stress seems to be lexically conditioned. It may fall on the first syllable of bisyllabic words: [...] In bisyllabic words, stress may also be on the second syllable, and this seems to be the case where at least the second syllable is closed and thus ’heavy’: [...] With trisyllabic words, stress is on the last syllable: [...] As noted above, stress in Vera’a still needs to be investigated in greater detail.
new_statements.citation: Schnell, Stefan. 2011. A grammar of Vera'a, an Oceanic language of North Vanuatu. Kiel: Kiel University (Ms., ix+211 pp.).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Author treats Vera'a word stress as free/lexical (explicitly preliminary). Observed tendencies: CV.CV bisyllables take initial stress ('rE.NE 'woman', 'la.ka 'dance'); bisyllables whose second syllable is closed take final stress (lak.'lak, va.'ʔal 'banana', ʔaŋ.'sar 'person'); trisyllables take final stress (ʔaŋ.sa.'ra, na.na.'ra); words like mi.'mi.je 'red', vu.'nuo 'island' with apparent penult stress are reanalysed as bisyllabic with a heavy vowel-sequence nucleus. A weight-sensitive right-edge analysis is suggested by the data but not asserted by the author.
new_statements.exceptions: Apparent penultimate stress in forms with vowel sequences plus epenthetic glide (mi.'mi.je, se.'se.jE, vu.'nuo, du.'ruo) attributed to heavy nuclei; author twice flags the whole section as preliminary. Note conflicting views elsewhere: François 2005:451 (comparative) says Torres-Banks languages generally have final stress; A. François (as Wikipedia user Womtelo, 2023 edit summary, unpublished) regards Vera'a as having lost stress altogether.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms with IPA stress marks; no discussion of phrase-level prosody or of stress on the elidable final echo vowel in phrase-medial position.
new_statements.identity_note: vatr1237 'Vatrata' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO code [vlr], split in 2009 (CR 2008-069) into Vera'a [vra] = vera1241 and Lemerig [lrz] = leme1238. The quoted statement (Schnell 2011) describes Vera'a (vera1241), the language of Vera'a/Vatrata village on west Vanua Lava, i.e. the principal referent of the old name; it should be cataloged under vera1241. No stress statement was found for Lemerig (leme1238). The Wikipedia claim 'There is no stress in Vera'a' (used by the earlier scan) is unsourced and traces to a 2023 Wikipedia edit summary by user Womtelo, not to Schnell 2011, which says the opposite (free/lexical stress, preliminary).

sources.quote: Stress still needs to be investigated in greater detail. However, some preliminary findings shall be outlined here. Stress is free in the sense that its position cannot be predicted for any word from general phonological rules. Stress seems to be lexically conditioned. It may fall on the first syllable of bisyllabic words: [...] In bisyllabic words, stress may also be on the second syllable, and this seems to be the case where at least the second syllable is closed and thus ’heavy’: [...] With trisyllabic words, stress is on the last syllable: [...] As noted above, stress in Vera’a still needs to be investigated in greater detail.
sources.note: Ch.2 Phonology, sec. 2.3 'Stress' (pp. 28-29): preliminary; stress is 'free', position not predictable by rule, 'lexically conditioned'; bisyllables with two light syllables stressed on the 1st, bisyllables with a closed 2nd syllable stressed on the 2nd; trisyllables stressed on the last syllable; apparent penult stress in vowel-sequence words (mi.'mi.je, vu.'nuo) reanalysed as heavy nuclei; 'still needs to be investigated in greater detail'.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2005. Unraveling the history of the vowels of seventeen northern Vanuatu languages. Oceanic Linguistics 44(2): 443-504.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative-historical. p.451: 'The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77).' Vera'a (VRA) and Lemerig (LMG) are among the 17; for Vera'a, pp.464-465 treat the final echo vowel Vf as 'a clone of the preceding stressed vowel' (i.e. stress on the last full vowel). No language-specific stress rule stated for Vera'a or Lemerig.
